title: EX2: the fast balance turns into one rate, k_obs = K_op k_ch
body:
## Why this node now

You can write $Q$ for $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$ and you know exchange happens only from $O$:

$$\frac{dX}{dt} = k_{ch}\,O.$$

That is the whole physics. But an HDX experiment does not see $O$. It sees one number: how fast the unexchanged pool $U = C + O$ drains, which it reports as a single rate $k_{obs}$ with $U(t) \approx U_0 e^{-k_{obs} t}$. So the question of this node is: **what is $O$, as a fraction of $U$, when opening and closing are fast?** Once we know that, $dX/dt = k_{ch} O$ becomes $dX/dt = k_{obs} U$ and we read off $k_{obs}$.

## The derivation, move by move

**Move 1: compare the time scales.** In a folded protein, a typical amide opens rarely ($k_{op} \sim 1$ per s or slower) and, once open, snaps shut fast ($k_{cl} \sim 100$ to $1000$ per s). Chemical exchange from the open state is slow at neutral pH ($k_{ch} \sim 1$ to $10$ per s). So an open site closes many times before it ever exchanges. The $C \rightleftharpoons O$ hop happens over and over; $O \to X$ is a rare leak out of that back-and-forth.

**Move 2: a fast back-and-forth settles to its balanced split.** You already solved this for the two-state chain: the stationary split has equal flows both ways, $k_{op}\,C = k_{cl}\,O$. Since the leak to $X$ is slow, the pair $C, O$ reaches that balance long before much has leaked. So at any moment during the experiment,

$$\frac{O}{C} = \frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl}} \equiv K_{op}.$$

$K_{op}$ is an equilibrium constant: the open fraction relative to closed. For a stable amide, $K_{op} \ll 1$.

**Move 3: express $O$ as a fraction of the unexchanged pool.** $U = C + O$, and with $K_{op} \ll 1$, $C \approx U$, so $O \approx K_{op} U$. (Exactly: $O = \frac{K_{op}}{1 + K_{op}} U$; the $1 + K_{op}$ in the denominator is where the general formula will differ, so keep it in mind.)

**Move 4: substitute into the exchange current.**

$$\frac{dX}{dt} = k_{ch}\,O \approx k_{ch} K_{op}\,U.$$

Every exchanged site came out of $U$, so $dU/dt = -dX/dt = -(K_{op} k_{ch})\,U$. That is $dS/dt = -kS$ with

$$k_{obs} = K_{op}\,k_{ch} = \frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl}}\,k_{ch}.$$

This is the **EX2** limit. The name just means "exchange regime 2": closing wins the race against exchange, so many openings are needed per exchange event.

## Worked instance, with numbers

$k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10$ per second, 1000 unexchanged sites.

1. Balance: $k_{op} C = k_{cl} O \Rightarrow O = C/100$. With $C + O = 1000$: $O \approx 10$ sites open at any instant (exactly $1000/101 \approx 9.9$).
2. Current: $dX/dt = k_{ch} O = 10 \times 10 = 100$ sites per second.
3. Rate: $k_{obs} = 100 / 1000 = 0.1$ per second. Check against the formula: $K_{op} k_{ch} = (1/100)\times 10 = 0.1$. Same.

Compare with $k_{op} = 1$: sites open once a second, yet exchange ten times slower. Why: each opening lasts about $1/(k_{cl} + k_{ch}) \approx 1/110$ s, and in that window exchange fires with probability about $k_{ch}/(k_{cl} + k_{ch}) = 10/110 \approx 0.09$. So roughly one opening in eleven pays off, and $k_{obs} \approx k_{op} \times 0.09 \approx 0.09$. The balance argument and the per-opening argument give the same answer; that is the sign the picture is right.

## What it hangs off

- $dX/dt = k_{ch} O$ (R1): exchange only from the open state.
- Flow balance $k_{op}\pi_C = k_{cl}\pi_O$ for the two-state chain, which you solved numerically last session ($0.1\pi_C = 0.3\pi_O \Rightarrow 750/250$). Here it is the same equation with rates instead of per-step probabilities.
- $dS/dt = -kS$ gives $e^{-kt}$: once the current is proportional to $U$, you have a single rate.

The one assumption to carry forward: **$C \rightleftharpoons O$ settles much faster than $O$ leaks.** D2 is what happens when that fails.

title: Why the balance holds: count what one opening does
body:
## The step that was missing

You wrote "since this is in equilibrium, $O/C$ is constant." True, but it is the conclusion, not the reason. The reason has to come from the rates, and it comes from looking at **one opening** and asking how it ends.

## One opening, two exits

Once a site is open, it has exactly two ways out: close at $k_{cl}$, or exchange at $k_{ch}$. Two competing exits from one state. You already know what that means from $Q$: the total exit rate is $k_{cl} + k_{ch}$, and the share of each exit is its rate over the total. So

$$P(\text{opening ends in exchange}) = \frac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl} + k_{ch}}, \qquad P(\text{opening ends in closing}) = \frac{k_{cl}}{k_{cl} + k_{ch}}.$$

Why this formula and not something else: in a short slice $dt$, the site exchanges with probability $k_{ch}\,dt$ and closes with probability $k_{cl}\,dt$. Given that *something* happened in the slice, the exchange share is $k_{ch}\,dt / (k_{cl}\,dt + k_{ch}\,dt)$, and the $dt$ cancels. The same ratio holds in every slice, so it holds for the opening as a whole.

## Worked numbers: $k_{cl} = 50$, $k_{ch} = 5$ per second

- Exchange share per opening: $5 / 55 \approx 0.09$. Out of 100 openings, about 9 exchange and about 91 close.
- So a typical site does $C \to O \to C \to O \to C \ldots$ about eleven times before a leak to $X$.
- The $C \rightleftharpoons O$ hop has therefore repeated many times before anything irreversible happens. A two-state hop that repeats many times settles to its balance $k_{op}C = k_{cl}O$ (this is the stationary split you solved last session). The leak to $X$ is then a slow drain *of an already balanced pool*.

That is what justifies $O/C = k_{op}/k_{cl}$ at every moment of the experiment.

## The comparison, stated as an inequality

The balance argument needs most openings to close rather than exchange:

$$k_{cl} \gg k_{ch}.$$

This is **not** the same as $k_{cl} \gg k_{op}$. That second inequality says $O$ is small compared with $C$ (useful for $C \approx U$), but says nothing about whether the pair has time to settle. Here is a case that separates them: $k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10^4$ per second (high pH). Still $k_{cl} \gg k_{op}$, so $O$ is tiny at any instant. But the exchange share per opening is $10^4 / (100 + 10^4) \approx 0.99$: almost every opening exchanges, the pair never gets to hop back and forth, and the balance argument fails. That is the EX1 side, which D2 covers.

## Where this hangs

- Competing exits from one state: the row of $Q$ for $O$ is $(k_{cl}, -(k_{cl}+k_{ch}), k_{ch})$; the exit shares are just those off-diagonal entries divided by the total exit.
- Stationary split of a two-state chain: $k_{op}\pi_C = k_{cl}\pi_O$, reached only if the chain hops many times.

The single fact to carry into D2: **the regime is decided by which exit of $O$ wins, closing or exchange.**

title: Two inequalities, two jobs: small O versus balanced O
body:
## What went wrong

You named $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$, which is the right one, and added $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$. Both are true in a folded protein, but they do different jobs, and only one of them is the EX2 condition. This distinction is the hinge for D2 and D4, so it is worth one page.

## The two jobs

**Job 1: how big is $O$?** From the balance $k_{op}C = k_{cl}O$, the open fraction is $O/C = k_{op}/k_{cl}$. If $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$, then $O \ll C$, which lets us write $C \approx U$. That is all $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$ does: it makes $O$ **small**.

**Job 2: does the pair have time to settle?** That is decided by what one opening does. An open site has two exits, close at $k_{cl}$ and exchange at $k_{ch}$, so the share of openings that end in exchange is

$$\frac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl} + k_{ch}}.$$

Notice: no $k_{op}$ anywhere in this. If this share is small, the site hops $C \rightleftharpoons O$ many times before a leak, and the pair settles to its balance. That requires $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$. It makes $O$ **balanced**.

## Worked example with the same $k_{op}, k_{cl}$ and two values of $k_{ch}$

$k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$ per second, 1000 sites.

**Case A: $k_{ch} = 10$.**
- Exchange share per opening: $10/110 \approx 0.09$. About eleven hops per leak, so the pair settles. Balance holds.
- Balanced split: $O/C = 1/100$, $O \approx 10$ sites.
- Current: $dX/dt = 10 \times 10 = 100$ per s, $k_{obs} = 0.1$ per s $= K_{op}k_{ch}$. EX2.

**Case B: $k_{ch} = 10^4$ (high pH, exchange chemistry very fast).**
- $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$ is still true, so at any instant $O$ is still tiny.
- But exchange share per opening: $10^4/10100 \approx 0.99$. The first opening almost always exchanges. The site never hops back; there is no repeated back-and-forth to settle. Balance **fails**.
- What happens instead: every opening is a one-way trip $C \to O \to X$, so $X$ grows at the rate sites open: $k_{obs} \approx k_{op} = 1$ per s. (That is D2.) Check that EX2 would have been absurd here: $K_{op}k_{ch} = 0.01 \times 10^4 = 100$ per s, a hundred times faster than sites even open.

Same $k_{op}$, same $k_{cl}$, same "$O$ is small" inequality. Only $k_{ch}$ changed, and it flipped the regime. So the regime is decided by $k_{ch}$ versus $k_{cl}$, full stop.

## One-line summary to carry

- $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$: $O$ is small ($C \approx U$). Not the regime condition.
- $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$: $O$ is balanced, $k_{obs} = K_{op}k_{ch}$. This is EX2.
- $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$: every opening exchanges, $k_{obs} = k_{op}$. This is EX1.

title: EX1: when every opening exchanges, k_obs = k_op
body:
## Why this node now

D1 rested on one assumption: closing beats exchange, $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$. You have just seen the assumption fail (Case B, $k_{ch} = 10^4$). This node asks: what is $k_{obs}$ on the other side? The answer is simpler than EX2, and you already guessed it.

## The derivation

**Move 1: what one opening does when exchange wins.** Exchange share per opening is $k_{ch}/(k_{cl} + k_{ch})$. If $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$, that share is close to 1: an open site exchanges before it can close. Each opening is a one-way trip $C \to O \to X$.

**Move 2: so the bottleneck is opening.** $X$ cannot grow faster than sites open, and now it grows exactly as fast as sites open, because nothing opened ever returns. The exchange current is the opening current:

$$\frac{dX}{dt} = k_{op}\,C.$$

**Move 3: $C$ is the unexchanged pool.** Sites that open leave $O$ almost instantly (exit rate $k_{cl} + k_{ch}$, huge), so $O \approx 0$ and $U = C + O \approx C$. Then $dU/dt = -k_{op} U$, a single rate:

$$k_{obs} = k_{op}.$$

This is **EX1**: the observed rate *is* the opening rate. The chemistry ($k_{ch}$) has dropped out entirely, and so has $k_{cl}$. Nothing about the closing or the chemistry can be read from the rate; only the opening dynamics.

**How you could have found it without Move 2.** Start from R1, $dX/dt = k_{ch} O$, and ask what $O$ is now. Open sites are created at $k_{op} C$ and destroyed at $(k_{cl} + k_{ch}) O$. Destruction is enormously fast, so $O$ stays at the tiny level where creation and destruction match: $O \approx k_{op} C/(k_{cl} + k_{ch})$. Substitute: $dX/dt = k_{ch} \cdot k_{op} C/(k_{cl} + k_{ch}) = k_{op} C \cdot \frac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl} + k_{ch}} \approx k_{op} C$ when $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$. Same answer, and notice the factor $\frac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$ is the exchange share per opening again. Keep this "creation equals destruction" move in mind: it is R2, and it will give the general formula in D3.

## Worked instance

$k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10^4$ per second, 1000 unexchanged sites.

1. Exchange share per opening: $10^4 / 10100 \approx 0.99$. Essentially every opening exchanges.
2. Opening current: $k_{op} C \approx 1 \times 1000 = 1000$ sites per second at $t = 0$.
3. Open sites present: $O \approx k_{op}C/(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) = 1000/10100 \approx 0.1$ sites. So $U \approx C$ to one part in ten thousand.
4. $k_{obs} = 1000/1000 = 1$ per second $= k_{op}$. The EX2 formula would have said $K_{op} k_{ch} = 0.01 \times 10^4 = 100$ per second, which is impossible: sites cannot exchange faster than they open.

## Where it hangs

- R1: $dX/dt = k_{ch} O$, exchange only from $O$.
- D1's hinge: the exchange share per opening $k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$. Near 0 gives EX2; near 1 gives EX1.
- The constraint in both regimes: $k_{obs} \le k_{op}$ always. EX1 is the case where the bound is reached.

The thing to notice for the boundary check: EX1 **needs** $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$. It does not need $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$; a stable protein and an unstable one both give $k_{obs} = k_{op}$ if exchange beats closing.

title: Steady state of a short-lived intermediate: dO/dt ≈ 0
body:
## Why this node now

D1 and D2 are the two ends. To get a formula that holds everywhere in between (D3), we need to know $O$ at every moment, not just in a limit. The master equation gives $O(t)$ exactly, but solving a $3 \times 3$ system is work. There is a shortcut that is both easier and more illuminating, and it rests on one fact about time scales. That fact is this node.

## The fact

Write the $O$ row of the master equation, which you can read straight off your $Q$:

$$\frac{dO}{dt} = k_{op}\,C - (k_{cl} + k_{ch})\,O.$$

Creation from $C$ at rate $k_{op}$ per closed site; destruction by the two exits of $O$, total $k_{cl} + k_{ch}$ per open site.

**Your guess of 1000 s was tracking the wrong pool.** $U$ drains over seconds (it is $e^{-k_{obs}t}$ with $k_{obs} \sim 0.1$ per s). But $O$ is a different animal: it is emptied at rate $k_{cl} + k_{ch}$, and a state emptied at rate $k$ has mean lifetime $1/k$. That is the same $e^{-kt}$ survival you derived for a single site: the fraction still in $O$ after time $t$ is $e^{-(k_{cl}+k_{ch})t}$, and the average of that lifetime is $1/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$.

So $O$ forgets its past in a time of order $1/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$. Whatever $O$ was a few of those lifetimes ago is gone; $O$ now is set entirely by the current supply $k_{op} C$. If the supply changes only slowly (and $C$ does, over seconds), $O$ tracks it: creation $\approx$ destruction at every instant,

$$\frac{dO}{dt} \approx 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad O \approx \frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl} + k_{ch}}\,C.$$

This is the **steady-state (quasi-stationary) approximation** for a short-lived intermediate. It is "unconditional" in the sense you need: whenever an intermediate is destroyed much faster than its supply changes, its population sits at creation $=$ destruction. Same move appears in enzyme kinetics (Michaelis–Menten) and in any chain reaction with a reactive intermediate.

## Worked instance

$k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10$ per second, 1000 sites all closed at $t = 0$.

1. Mean open lifetime: $1/(100 + 10) = 1/110$ s $\approx 9$ ms. So $O$ settles within a few tens of milliseconds.
2. Settled level: $O \approx k_{op} C/(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) = 1 \times 1000 / 110 \approx 9$ sites.
3. Check the two rates at that level: creation $= 1 \times 991 \approx 991$ per s; destruction $= 110 \times 9 = 990$ per s. Balanced.
4. Meanwhile $U$ drains at $k_{obs} \approx 0.1$ per s, a time scale of 10 s. Over the 9 ms it takes $O$ to settle, $U$ changes by $0.1 \times 0.009 \approx 0.1\%$. That gap, 9 ms versus 10 s, is why $dO/dt \approx 0$ is safe here.

Compare with D1: there we used $k_{op}C = k_{cl}O$ and got $O \approx 10$. Here we get $O \approx 9$. The difference is the $k_{ch}$ in the denominator: the steady state counts *both* exits of $O$, not just closing. D1 ignored $k_{ch}$ there because it was small compared with $k_{cl}$. The steady state does not need that; it works in EX1 too.

## Where it hangs

- The $O$ row of $Q$: creation and destruction terms you already write.
- Mean lifetime $1/k$ of a state with exit rate $k$, from $e^{-kt}$.
- The separation of time scales: $O$ settles in $\sim 1/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$, $U$ drains in $\sim 1/k_{obs}$, and the first is much shorter.

The boundary to keep in mind: $dO/dt \approx 0$ fails if the supply changes as fast as $O$ forgets, i.e. if $k_{obs}$ is comparable to $k_{cl}+k_{ch}$. Since $k_{obs} \le k_{op}$, that needs $k_{op}$ comparable to $k_{cl}+k_{ch}$: an unstable amide that is open half the time. For a folded protein it does not happen.

title: Steady state, worked once more, with the checks a careful hand does
body:
## What this page is for

Your steady-state expression was right: $O \approx k_{op}C/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$. The number came out wrong at the division. That is attention, not understanding, and attention is trained by building in checks. So here is the same computation done the way a careful hand does it: every number gets a cheap independent check before it is trusted.

## Worked instance: $k_{op} = 3$, $k_{cl} = 400$, $k_{ch} = 50$ per second, 1000 sites nearly all closed

**Step 1: total exit rate from $O$.** Two exits, close at 400 and exchange at 50: $k_{cl} + k_{ch} = 450$ per second. *Check:* it must exceed the larger of the two (450 > 400). Yes.

**Step 2: mean open lifetime.** $1/450$ s $\approx 0.0022$ s, about 2 ms. *Check by rounding:* $1/500 = 0.002$ and $1/400 = 0.0025$; the answer must sit between them. $0.0022$ does.

**Step 3: steady-state open count.** Creation equals destruction: $k_{op}C = (k_{cl}+k_{ch})\,O$, so

$$O \approx \frac{3 \times 1000}{450} = \frac{3000}{450}.$$

*Check by rounding before dividing:* $3000/500 = 6$ and $3000/400 = 7.5$, so the answer must lie between 6 and 7.5. Now divide: $3000/450 = 6.67$. In range. (Had I written 3.33, the rounding check would have caught it immediately: 3.33 is below 6.)

**Step 4: second independent check, the lifetime route.** Open sites $=$ (openings per second) $\times$ (mean open lifetime) $= k_{op}C \times \frac{1}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}} = 3000 \times 0.0022 \approx 6.7$. Same number, computed in a different order. This is Little's law: population equals arrival rate times residence time. Two routes agreeing is the strongest check there is.

**Step 5: plausibility against $U$.** $O/U \approx 6.7/1000 \approx 0.7\%$. Small, as it must be for a folded amide with $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}$. If $O$ had come out as 300, something would be wrong.

## The habit to take away

Before you trust a division, bracket it with two easy ones (round the denominator up and down). Before you trust a steady-state count, recompute it as rate $\times$ lifetime. Each check costs ten seconds and catches exactly the kind of slip that cost you the last answer. The grader does not care about arithmetic for its own sake; it matters because an open-site count that is off by a factor of 2 becomes a $k_{obs}$ off by a factor of 2, and in HDX that is the difference between two regimes.

## Where it hangs

- Creation $k_{op}C$ and destruction $(k_{cl}+k_{ch})O$: the $O$ row of $Q$.
- Mean lifetime $1/k$ for exit rate $k$.
- Little's law, population $=$ rate $\times$ lifetime, is just the steady state read as a sentence.

title: A short-lived state fills up fast: dO/dt ≈ 0
body:
## Why this node now

You have two answers for $k_{obs}$: $K_{op} k_{ch}$ when closing is fast (EX2) and $k_{op}$ when exchange is fast (EX1). They were derived by two different stories. One formula should contain both, and the tool that gives it is the fact on this page. It is also the fact your pretest guess missed, so it is worth getting straight.

## Two clocks, not one

Look at the equation for $O$ alone. From the rate matrix $Q$ you already wrote:

$$\frac{dO}{dt} = k_{op} C - (k_{cl} + k_{ch})\, O$$

Inflow from $C$, outflow to $C$ and to $X$. Now ask the question you would ask of any one-exit-rate population: how fast does $O$ respond? The outflow term is $-(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) O$, the same shape as $dU/dt = -kU$, which you can already solve. So $O$ relaxes toward whatever the inflow supports with time constant

$$\tau_O = \frac{1}{k_{cl} + k_{ch}}$$

With $k_{cl} = 100$ and $k_{ch} = 10$ per second, $\tau_O = 1/110$ s, about $9$ ms. That is one clock.

The other clock is how fast the *unexchanged population* drains: $1/k_{obs}$. With $k_{obs} = 0.1$ per second that is $10$ s. In your guess you used this second clock to answer a question about the first. The two differ by a factor of a thousand, and that factor is the whole point.

## Why $dO/dt \approx 0$ follows

If $O$ adjusts in $9$ ms but its inflow $k_{op} C$ only changes on a $10$ s scale, then from $O$'s point of view the inflow is constant. A population with constant inflow and first-order outflow goes to the level where the two match and stays there. So after the first few $\tau_O$:

$$k_{op} C \approx (k_{cl} + k_{ch})\, O \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{dO}{dt} \approx 0$$

This is not "equilibrium". $C$ is still slowly draining into $X$. It is a *steady state of the fast variable*: $O$ tracks $C$ so closely that its own derivative is negligible next to its inflow and outflow, which are each about $1000$ per second while $dO/dt$ is at most a few per second. The name in chemistry is the steady-state approximation, and the condition for it is just that $O$'s relaxation is much faster than everything else: $k_{cl} + k_{ch} \gg k_{obs}$.

Notice what this does *not* need. It does not need $k_{cl} \gg k_{ch}$ (that was EX2) or $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$ (EX1). It only needs $O$ to be short-lived compared with the exchange time, which in practice is always true because $k_{op}$ is small. That is why it will give the general formula on the next page.

## Worked instance

$k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10$ per second, 1000 sites all closed at $t = 0$.

1. **Inflow at the start:** $k_{op} C = 1 \times 1000 = 1000$ open sites created per second. Reason: every closed site opens at rate $k_{op}$.
2. **Outflow per open site:** $k_{cl} + k_{ch} = 110$ per second. Reason: an open site has exactly two exits, and rates of independent exits add.
3. **Level:** inflow equals outflow when $1000 = 110\, O$, so $O \approx 9$ sites. Reason: that is the only $O$ at which $dO/dt = 0$.
4. **Time to get there:** $\tau_O = 1/110 \approx 9$ ms. After $30$ ms (three time constants) $O$ is within $5\%$ of $9$. Reason: $O$ relaxes like $1 - e^{-t/\tau_O}$, the same curve as $1 - e^{-kt}$.
5. **Check that $C$ hardly moved meanwhile:** in $30$ ms, exchanged sites are about $k_{obs} \times 0.03 \times 1000 = 3$. So $C$ is still $\approx 988$, and the inflow is still $\approx 1000$. The approximation is self-consistent.
6. **Sanity check on the level:** $O/C \approx 9/990 \approx 0.009$, close to $k_{op}/k_{cl} = 0.01$. The small difference is the $k_{ch}$ in the denominator, $k_{op}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) = 1/110$. That extra term is exactly what the EX2 story dropped, and it is what the general formula keeps.

## What it hangs off

Two things you already own. First, $dU/dt = -kU$ relaxes on the time $1/k$: here the "$k$" for $O$ is its total exit rate $k_{cl}+k_{ch}$. Second, the row of $Q$ for $O$, which you wrote in the pretest: the diagonal entry $-(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$ is minus the total exit rate, and that same number is what sets $O$'s clock.

title: Steady state of a short-lived intermediate: dO/dt ≈ 0
body:
## Why we need this now

You have two limits of the chain $C \rightleftharpoons O \to X$ and each came from a different argument. EX2 ($k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$) used "the $C \rightleftharpoons O$ balance is barely disturbed", giving $k_{obs} = K_{op}k_{ch}$. EX1 ($k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$) used "every opening exchanges", giving $k_{obs} = k_{op}$. Two separate stories is exactly the disconnected-facts situation. We want one formula that produces both. The tool that does it is a single approximation about $O$, and you just predicted it: **$O$ never piles up**.

## The idea, discovered

Write the exact balance for $O$ straight from the rate matrix you already own. Inflow is openings from $C$; outflow is closings and exchanges from $O$:

$$\frac{dO}{dt} = k_{op}\,C \;-\; (k_{cl} + k_{ch})\,O .$$

Now ask: how long does a molecule stay in $O$ once it gets there? Its total exit rate is $k_{cl} + k_{ch}$, so its mean lifetime is $1/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$. Compare that to how fast $C$ itself changes, which is at most on the timescale $1/k_{op}$ (that's how fast $C$ is being drained). If

$$k_{cl} + k_{ch} \;\gg\; k_{op},$$

then $O$ relaxes far faster than $C$ moves. Picture a bucket ($O$) with a tiny inlet ($k_{op}C$) and a huge drain ($(k_{cl}+k_{ch})O$). The water level settles in a blink to whatever height makes drain equal inlet, and from then on it just *tracks* the slowly changing inlet. Settled means not changing:

$$\frac{dO}{dt} \approx 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad O \approx \frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}\,C .$$

That is the **steady-state (quasi-stationary) approximation**. It does not say $O$ is constant forever; it says $O$ is always at its settled value *for the current* $C$. The error you make is the brief initial transient, of duration about $1/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$, during which the bucket fills.

Notice what the condition does **not** require. It does not need $k_{cl} \gg k_{ch}$ (EX2) or $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$ (EX1). Either exit can be the big one. All it needs is that the *sum* of exits from $O$ dwarfs the inflow rate constant $k_{op}$. For backbone amides that is essentially always true: openings are rare, and an open amide either snaps shut or exchanges within milliseconds to seconds.

## One worked instance

Take $k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10$ per second, all sites in $C$ at $t = 0$.

1. Total exit rate from $O$: $k_{cl}+k_{ch} = 110$ per second. Mean lifetime of an open state: $1/110 \approx 0.009$ s. *Reason: lifetime is the reciprocal of the total exit rate, the $1/k$ you already have.*
2. Compare with the inflow rate constant $k_{op} = 1$ per second: $110 \gg 1$, so the approximation applies. *Reason: $O$ drains about a hundred times faster than $C$ can be depleted.*
3. Settled value: $O \approx \dfrac{1}{110}\,C \approx 0.0091\,C$. *Reason: set $dO/dt = 0$ in the balance and solve.*
4. Check it is small and tracks $C$: at the start $C \approx 1$ so $O \approx 0.009$. When later $C$ has dropped to $0.5$, $O$ has already followed down to $\approx 0.0045$, because the re-settling takes only $\sim 0.01$ s while $C$ halving takes seconds.

Your prediction (b) was exactly this: a small, nearly constant $O$ that slides down with $C$.

## What it hangs off

Only $R1$: the balance equation for $O$ is the $O$-row of the master equation $\dot p = pQ$ you wrote with numbers, and "lifetime $= 1/(\text{total exit rate})$" is the same fact as $Q_{OO} = -(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$ being minus the total exit rate. The new ingredient is one move: when a state's exits are much faster than its inflow, set its time derivative to zero and solve algebraically. Next node, we feed this $O$ into $dX/dt = k_{ch}O$ and get $k_{obs}$ for every regime at once.

title: The general k_obs = k_op k_ch / (k_op + k_cl + k_ch)
body:
## Why now

We have the settled $O$. Exchange happens only from $O$ at rate $k_{ch}$ ($R1$: $dX/dt = k_{ch}O$). Put the two together and $k_{obs}$ drops out for *any* values of the three rates. EX1 and EX2 will then be two corners of one formula instead of two separate stories.

## The derivation

Unexchanged sites are $U = C + O$. Since $O$ is tiny compared with $C$ under the steady-state condition, $U \approx C$. The exchange flux is

$$\frac{dX}{dt} = k_{ch}\,O \approx k_{ch}\,\frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}\,C \approx \frac{k_{op}k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}\,U .$$

So $U$ decays as $dU/dt = -k_{obs}U$ with

$$k_{obs} \approx \frac{k_{op}\,k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}} .$$

Two readings of the same expression, both worth holding:

- **Product form:** $k_{obs} = k_{op}\cdot\dfrac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$. Openings happen at $k_{op}$; each opening exchanges with probability $\dfrac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$, the share of exits from $O$ that go to $X$ rather than back to $C$. (You used exactly this share when you found $k_{op}/2$ for $k_{ch} = k_{cl}$.)
- **Limits:** if $k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$ the share is $\approx k_{ch}/k_{cl}$ and $k_{obs} \to K_{op}k_{ch}$ (EX2). If $k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$ the share is $\approx 1$ and $k_{obs} \to k_{op}$ (EX1). Both earlier nodes fall out.

The full textbook formula has one more term in the denominator:

$$k_{obs} = \frac{k_{op}\,k_{ch}}{k_{op}+k_{cl}+k_{ch}} .$$

Where does the extra $k_{op}$ come from? From dropping the approximation $U \approx C$. Exactly, $U = C + O = C\left(1 + \frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}\right) = C\,\frac{k_{op}+k_{cl}+k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$, so $C = U\,\frac{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}{k_{op}+k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$. Substituting into $dX/dt = k_{ch}\frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}C$ gives the three-term denominator. When $k_{op} \ll k_{cl}+k_{ch}$, which is the steady-state condition itself, the extra term is negligible and the two forms agree. So the three-term formula is just the two-term one with the small correction for the few sites sitting in $O$ counted as still unexchanged.

## Worked instance

$k_{op} = 2$, $k_{cl} = 30$, $k_{ch} = 70$ per second (your numbers from the last node).

1. Exchange share per opening: $\dfrac{70}{30+70} = 0.7$. *Reason: of every 100 exits from $O$, 70 go to $X$.*
2. $k_{obs} = k_{op}\times 0.7 = 1.4$ per second. *Reason: openings at 2/s, 70% of them exchange.*
3. Three-term check: $\dfrac{2\cdot 70}{2+30+70} = \dfrac{140}{102} \approx 1.37$ per second. *Reason: the $2$ in the denominator is the $O$ correction, a 2% effect because $k_{op}$ is 2% of the exits.*
4. Regime: neither limit cleanly. $k_{ch} > k_{cl}$ so it leans EX1 ($k_{obs}$ is 70% of $k_{op}$, not 100%), and far from EX2 ($K_{op}k_{ch} = 4.7$/s would be badly wrong).

## What it hangs off

$R1$ supplies $dX/dt = k_{ch}O$. $R2$ supplies $O \approx \frac{k_{op}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}C$. $D1$ and $D2$ are the two corners you had already derived separately; now they are consequences, not assumptions. The only move added is multiplying the two and recognising the result as a first-order decay of $U$.

title: The race k_cl vs k_ch picks the regime; pH turns the k_ch knob
body:
## Why now

The general formula is in hand:

$$k_{obs} = k_{op}\cdot\frac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}} .$$

The second factor is the whole story of EX1 versus EX2. It is the probability that an open site exchanges before it closes, and it is decided by a **race** between two exits from $O$: closing at $k_{cl}$ and exchange at $k_{ch}$. Whichever is faster wins most of the time. This node makes that race explicit and then asks the practical question: in an experiment, which of these rates can you actually turn?

## The race, from the formula

Look at the share $\dfrac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$ as a function of the single ratio $r = k_{ch}/k_{cl}$:

$$\text{share} = \frac{r}{1+r}.$$

- $r \ll 1$ (closing wins): share $\approx r = k_{ch}/k_{cl}$, so $k_{obs} \approx k_{op}k_{ch}/k_{cl} = K_{op}k_{ch}$. **EX2.** A site opens and closes many times before one opening finally exchanges. $k_{obs}$ is proportional to $k_{ch}$, and it reports the *equilibrium* $K_{op}$, i.e. the stability $\Delta G_{op} = -RT\ln K_{op}$.
- $r \gg 1$ (exchange wins): share $\approx 1$, so $k_{obs} \approx k_{op}$. **EX1.** The first opening exchanges. $k_{obs}$ no longer depends on $k_{ch}$ at all, and it reports the *kinetics* of opening.
- $r = 1$: share $= 1/2$, the crossover. This is the $k_{op}/2$ you computed when $k_{ch} = k_{cl}$.

So the regime is not a property of the protein alone and not of the chemistry alone. It is a property of the ratio $k_{ch}/k_{cl}$.

## Which knob can you turn? pH

$k_{op}$ and $k_{cl}$ belong to the protein's dynamics; you can nudge them with temperature or denaturant, but not cleanly. $k_{ch}$ is different: it is the chemistry of an exposed amide, and above about pH 3 it is **base-catalysed**: the rate-limiting step is attack by $\mathrm{OH^-}$ on the amide N–H. Since $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$ rises ten-fold per pH unit,

$$k_{ch} \propto [\mathrm{OH^-}] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k_{ch} \text{ increases about } 10\times \text{ per pH unit.}$$

Orders of magnitude to hold: for a fully exposed amide at room temperature, $k_{ch}$ is of order $1$–$10$ per second at pH 7, about ten-fold more per unit above, and it bottoms out near pH 2.5–3 (which, together with $0\,^\circ$C, is why the quench in HDX-MS slows exchange by roughly four to five orders of magnitude).

Consequence: raising pH pushes **every** site toward EX1, because $k_{ch}$ climbs while $k_{cl}$ stays put. The pH at which a given site crosses over is the pH where $k_{ch}$ reaches that site's $k_{cl}$. Experimentally this is the standard test: if $k_{obs}$ scales ten-fold per pH unit, the site is EX2; if $k_{obs}$ stops responding to pH, it has gone EX1.

## Worked instance

A site with $k_{op} = 0.01$ per second and $k_{cl} = 100$ per second ($K_{op} = 10^{-4}$, a well-protected amide). Take $k_{ch} = 10$ per second at pH 7.

1. **pH 7:** $r = 10/100 = 0.1$. Share $= 0.1/1.1 \approx 0.09$. $k_{obs} = 0.01 \times 0.09 \approx 9\times10^{-4}$ per second. *Reason: closing wins 10 to 1; EX2, and indeed $K_{op}k_{ch} = 10^{-4}\times 10 = 10^{-3}$ is within 10%.*
2. **pH 8:** $k_{ch} = 100$ per second, $r = 1$. Share $= 0.5$. $k_{obs} = 0.005$ per second. *Reason: the crossover; one pH unit multiplied $k_{ch}$ by 10 but $k_{obs}$ by only about 5, the first sign of leaving EX2.*
3. **pH 9:** $k_{ch} = 1000$ per second, $r = 10$. Share $\approx 0.91$. $k_{obs} \approx 0.0091$ per second. *Reason: exchange now wins 10 to 1; EX1, $k_{obs} \to k_{op} = 0.01$.*
4. **pH 10:** $k_{ch} = 10^4$, share $\approx 0.99$, $k_{obs} \approx 0.0099$. *Reason: saturated at $k_{op}$; another pH unit changed $k_{obs}$ by 9%.*

Across pH 7 to 10, $k_{ch}$ rose a thousand-fold but $k_{obs}$ rose only eleven-fold, from $9\times10^{-4}$ to $0.0099$ per second, and flattened. That flattening *is* the EX2 to EX1 transition, and its location told you $k_{cl} \approx 100$ per second.

## What it hangs off

Entirely off D3. Nothing new is derived; the share $k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$ is simply reread as the outcome of a race, and one external fact is attached: $k_{ch}$ is the only one of the three rates with a clean experimental knob, and that knob is pH, ten-fold per unit.

title: Envelope shape: gradual shift (EX2) versus bimodal (EX1)
body:
## Why now

Everything so far was one amide. A mass spectrometer sees a **peptide** with $N$ exchangeable amides, and what it reports is the isotope envelope: a histogram of how many deuterons each peptide molecule carries. The question this whole lesson was aimed at: why does EX2 produce an envelope that slides gradually to higher mass, while EX1 produces two peaks whose heights trade places? The answer is a direct consequence of the race, applied to $N$ sites that open together.

## The setup

Take a segment of $N$ amides that opens and closes **as a unit** (a cooperative unfolding event: the whole helix or hairpin frays at once). Every opening exposes all $N$ sites at the same time, for a lifetime of order $1/(k_{cl}+k_{ch})$. Ask of one opening event: how many of the $N$ sites exchange before the segment closes?

Each exposed site independently runs its own race against the same closing clock. The probability a given site exchanges during this opening is the share $s = \dfrac{k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$.

## EX1: all or nothing per opening

$k_{ch} \gg k_{cl}$, so $s \approx 1$. In a single opening, essentially **all $N$ sites exchange**. A peptide molecule is therefore in one of two states: never yet opened (mass $+0$) or opened at least once (mass $+N$). Nothing in between exists, because an opening is never partial. The fraction that has opened by time $t$ is $1 - e^{-k_{op}t}$, so the envelope is **two peaks at fixed positions**, $+0$ and $+N$, with the low-mass peak draining into the high-mass peak at rate $k_{op}$. That is the bimodal signature. The peaks do not move; only their heights change.

## EX2: a tiny bite per opening

$k_{ch} \ll k_{cl}$, so $s \ll 1$. In a single opening, each site exchanges with small probability $s$, independently of its neighbours. A typical opening exchanges zero or one site. Exchange is accumulated over **many** openings ($\sim 1/s$ of them per site), and because each site's successes are independent coin flips across openings, after time $t$ each site is exchanged with probability

$$p(t) = 1 - e^{-k_{obs}t}, \qquad k_{obs} = K_{op}k_{ch},$$

independently of the others. The number of deuterons on a peptide is then **binomial**, $\mathrm{Bin}(N, p)$: a single hump centred at $Np$ with width $\sqrt{Np(1-p)}$. As $t$ grows the hump **slides** from $0$ to $N$ through every intermediate position. That is the gradual, unimodal shift.

The key dependency: independence of sites comes from $s \ll 1$. When each opening exchanges at most one site, which sites exchange is uncorrelated, and a sum of $N$ independent coin flips is a binomial. When $s \approx 1$, every opening exchanges all sites, the coin flips are perfectly correlated, and the distribution collapses to two spikes. Both envelopes have the **same centroid**, $N(1 - e^{-k_{obs}t})$; only the shape distinguishes them. Centroid-only analysis cannot tell EX1 from EX2. The envelope width can.

## Worked instance

$N = 10$ sites, $t$ chosen so that half the exchange is done, $k_{obs}t = \ln 2$ (e.g. $k_{obs} = 0.01$ per second, $t \approx 69$ s).

- **EX2:** $p = 0.5$ for each site. Deuteron count $\sim \mathrm{Bin}(10, 0.5)$: mean $5$, standard deviation $\sqrt{10\times0.25} \approx 1.6$. One peak centred at $+5$, spanning roughly $+2$ to $+8$. *Reason: 10 independent fair coins.*
- **EX1:** with $k_{op} = 0.01$ per second, half the molecules have opened. Half the intensity at $+0$, half at $+10$, nothing at $+5$. *Reason: each opening exchanges all 10 sites, so each molecule is all-or-nothing.* Centroid also $+5$.

Same centroid, opposite shapes. In an experiment, a stretched or bimodal envelope that persists over several time points, especially at raised pH, is the fingerprint of EX1 and hence of a cooperative opening whose $k_{op}$ you can read directly.

## What it hangs off

D4 supplies the share $s$ and the fact that pH pushes $s \to 1$. D2 supplies "every opening exchanges" for EX1 and D1 "many openings per exchange" for EX2. The one new idea is statistical: $N$ sites that open together are $N$ coin flips with success probability $s$ per opening, independent when $s \ll 1$ and perfectly correlated when $s \approx 1$. Independent flips give a binomial hump; correlated flips give two spikes.

title: The two handles: the scalar ODE and the eigenvector equation
body:
## Why these two, now

Everything in this lesson is built by combining exactly two facts you already own, so it is worth stating them in the precise form we will use. Nothing else is needed: no new theorems, no linear algebra beyond what these say.

## Handle 1: the scalar linear ODE

$$\frac{dc}{dt} = \lambda c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c(t) = c(0)\,e^{\lambda t}.$$

This is $dS/dt = -kS$ with $\lambda = -k$. Two things to hold explicitly:

- **It is the only solution.** If $c(0)$ is given, $c(t)$ is fixed for all $t$. (Reason: the ODE tells you the slope at every point, so from the starting value the curve is traced out with no freedom. Formally, $\frac{d}{dt}\left(c\,e^{-\lambda t}\right) = \dot c e^{-\lambda t} - \lambda c e^{-\lambda t} = 0$, so $c\,e^{-\lambda t}$ is constant, equal to $c(0)$.)
- **The sign of $\lambda$ is the whole story.** $\lambda < 0$: decays at rate $|\lambda|$, lifetime $1/|\lambda|$. $\lambda = 0$: $c$ stays at $c(0)$ forever. $\lambda > 0$: grows. For rate matrices only the first two occur.

## Handle 2: the eigenvector equation, in the row convention

For the master equation you write populations as a **row** $p = (p_C, p_O, p_X)$ and $\dot p = pQ$, with $Q_{ij}$ the rate from $i$ to $j$. Because $p$ multiplies from the left, the relevant eigenvectors are **left** eigenvectors, rows $v$ with

$$vQ = \lambda v, \qquad v \neq 0.$$

In words: $Q$ acting on $v$ gives back $v$, scaled by the number $\lambda$. The direction survives, only the length changes. ($v \neq 0$ is required because $0 \cdot Q = \lambda \cdot 0$ for every $\lambda$, which would make every number an eigenvalue.) Left and right eigenvectors have the same eigenvalues, since $\det(Q - \lambda I) = \det(Q^T - \lambda I)$, so the characteristic polynomial you computed yesterday is the same either way. Only the vectors differ.

Eigenvalues of a rate matrix carry the units of $Q$: per second. Keep that in view; it is the fastest way to catch "eigenvalue = population" type errors.

## One worked instance

$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$ per second, two states, rates $1 \to 2$ at $1$/s and $2 \to 1$ at $4$/s. You found $\lambda^2 + 5\lambda = 0$, so $\lambda = 0$ and $\lambda = -5$.

1. **Left eigenvector for $\lambda = 0$.** Solve $vQ = 0$ with $v = (a, b)$: first component $-a + 4b = 0$, so $a = 4b$. Take $v_0 = (4, 1)$. *Reason: $vQ = 0$ is the same as $\dot p = 0$ for $p \propto v$, so this row is the stationary split: 80% in state 1, 20% in state 2. Check the flux balance: $1 \times 4 = 4 \times 1$.* That is your prediction made precise: the $\lambda = 0$ direction is not any population, it is the one split that balances every flux.
2. **Left eigenvector for $\lambda = -5$.** Solve $vQ = -5v$: first component $-a + 4b = -5a$, so $4a = -4b$, $b = -a$. Take $v_1 = (1, -1)$. Check the second component: $a - 4b = 1 + 4 = 5 = -5 \times (-1)$. *Reason: this row has total $0$; it moves population from state 2 to state 1 without changing the sum. It is the "imbalance" direction.*
3. **Lifetime.** Along $v_1$, Handle 1 says the imbalance decays as $e^{-5t}$: relaxation time $0.2$ s. Notice $5 = 1 + 4$, the sum of the two rates, as you would expect for a two-state relaxation.

## What it hangs off

Handle 1 is the $k\,dt$ rule integrated. Handle 2 is the eigenvector definition you gave yesterday, restated for rows because $p$ sits on the left of $Q$. The next node puts them together: what happens to $\dot p = pQ$ when $p$ points along $v_1$.

title: Along an eigenvector, the matrix equation collapses to the scalar one
body:
## Why now

$\dot p = pQ$ is three coupled equations: $\dot p_C$ depends on $p_O$, $\dot p_O$ on $p_C$, and so on. You cannot solve one without the others. The scalar handle $\dot c = \lambda c$ is uncoupled and trivial. The question that drives this whole lesson is: **is there any starting population for which the coupled system behaves like the uncoupled one?** If so, we have a foothold.

## The discovery

Guess the simplest possible shape: all populations proportional to one fixed row, $p(t) = c(t)\,v$, with $v$ constant and only the overall scale $c(t)$ changing. Feed that guess into both sides of $\dot p = pQ$ and see what it demands.

- **Left side.** $v$ does not depend on time, so $\dot p = \dot c\,v$.
- **Right side.** $pQ = (c\,v)Q = c\,(vQ)$. For the guess to close, $vQ$ must again be a multiple of $v$, otherwise the right side points in a new direction and $p$ cannot stay proportional to $v$. So the guess works **exactly when $v$ is a left eigenvector**: $vQ = \lambda v$. Then $pQ = c\lambda\,v$.

Both sides are multiples of the same row $v$, so match the multipliers:

$$\dot c\,v = \lambda c\,v \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dot c = \lambda c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c(t) = c(0)\,e^{\lambda t}.$$

The matrix has vanished. Along an eigenvector, the three coupled equations are one scalar equation whose rate is the eigenvalue. The eigenvector is the **shape** that is preserved; the eigenvalue is the **rate** at which that shape's amplitude decays. That is why the eigenvalues of $Q$ are rates (per second) and never populations.

Notice what was *not* allowed: writing $e^{Qt}$ and treating $Q$ as a number. We never divided by $Q$ or took its logarithm. We only used $vQ = \lambda v$ to replace a matrix product by a scalar product, and then Handle 1.

## Worked instance

$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$ per second, with $v_1 = (1, -1)$ and $v_1 Q = -5\,v_1$ from the last page.

Start at $p(0) = 0.1\,v_1 = (0.1, -0.1)$. (Negative population is fine here: this is a *deviation* from the stationary split, and deviations can have either sign. We add the stationary part back in the next node.)

1. Assume $p(t) = c(t)\,(1,-1)$ with $c(0) = 0.1$. *Reason: trying the one shape that $Q$ preserves.*
2. $\dot p = \dot c\,(1,-1)$. *Reason: the row is constant.*
3. $pQ = c\,(1,-1)Q = c\,(-5)(1,-1) = -5c\,(1,-1)$. *Reason: the eigenvector equation, verified on the last page.*
4. Match: $\dot c = -5c$, so $c(t) = 0.1\,e^{-5t}$. *Reason: Handle 1.*
5. Therefore $p(t) = (0.1\,e^{-5t},\ -0.1\,e^{-5t})$. Check at $t = 0.2$ s: $c = 0.1\,e^{-1} \approx 0.037$. The deviation has shrunk to 37% of its start in one lifetime $1/5$ s, both components together, shape intact.

Compare with what a wrong move gives: writing $p(t) = e^{Qt}$ with $Q$ left as a matrix produces no number at all for $p_1(0.2)$. The eigenvector route gives $0.037$.

## What it hangs off

Handle 2 ($vQ = \lambda v$) is what lets the right side be rewritten as a scalar times $v$. Handle 1 then solves the scalar equation. The only new idea is the *guess* $p = c\,v$, motivated by asking which starting shapes make the coupled system uncoupled. Next node: a general $p(0)$ is not an eigenvector, but it is a sum of them, and the equation is linear.

title: Along an eigenvector the matrix ODE becomes a scalar ODE
body:
## Why this node now

The master equation $\dot p = pQ$ is a system of coupled ODEs: every component of $p$ feeds every other through $Q$. You already own one ODE completely, the scalar one, $\dot c = \lambda c$, whose solution is $c(t) = c(0)\,e^{\lambda t}$. The whole strategy of this lesson is: find the directions in which the coupled system *is secretly* that scalar equation. Those directions are the eigenvectors. This node shows why.

## The move you could have discovered

Ask: for which $p$ is the right-hand side $pQ$ easy? The right-hand side is a matrix acting on a vector, and in general it points somewhere new. But by definition, a left eigenvector $v \neq 0$ with $vQ = \lambda v$ is a direction that $Q$ does *not* turn: it only stretches it by $\lambda$. So suppose at some moment $p$ lies along $v$:

$$p(t) = c(t)\,v,$$

with $c(t)$ a scalar and $v$ a fixed vector (it does not depend on time). Now substitute into **both sides** of $\dot p = pQ$, one side at a time. Keeping the two sides separate is exactly the step that slipped last time.

**Left side.** $v$ is constant, so differentiating $p = c\,v$ only differentiates $c$:
$$\dot p = \dot c\, v.$$

**Right side.** Replace $p$ by $c\,v$, then pull the scalar $c$ out in front (scalars commute with everything), then use the eigenvector equation:
$$pQ = (c\,v)Q = c\,(vQ) = c\,(\lambda v) = \lambda c\, v.$$

Note the bookkeeping: $pQ$ is not $c\,v$. It is $c$ times $vQ$, and *only then* does $vQ = \lambda v$ get used to replace $vQ$ by $\lambda v$.

**Equate.** $\dot c\, v = \lambda c\, v$. Both sides are multiples of the same nonzero vector $v$, so the scalar coefficients must match:
$$\dot c = \lambda c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c(t) = c(0)\,e^{\lambda t}.$$

This is where $v \neq 0$ earns its place in the definition: if $v$ were the zero vector, $\dot c\,v = \lambda c\,v$ would say $0 = 0$ and tell us nothing about $c$.

**Conclusion.** If $p$ starts along an eigenvector, it stays along it forever, and its length just scales as $e^{\lambda t}$:
$$p(t) = c(0)\,e^{\lambda t}\,v.$$

For a rate matrix, $\lambda = 0$ gives a mode that never changes (the stationary split you found last time), and $\lambda < 0$ gives a mode that decays with rate $|\lambda|$.

## One worked instance

Take the $Q$ from last time:
$$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{eigenvalues } 0 \text{ and } -5.$$

Find the left eigenvector for $\lambda = -5$. We need $vQ = -5v$. Try $v = (1, -1)$:
$$vQ = (1\cdot(-1) + (-1)\cdot 4,\; 1\cdot 1 + (-1)\cdot(-4)) = (-5,\; 5) = -5\,(1,-1). \checkmark$$

Now set $p(0) = 0.3\,(1,-1) = (0.3, -0.3)$. (Not a probability vector by itself; it is a *deviation* from the stationary split. That is fine, the equation is linear.)

- Left side: $\dot p = \dot c\,(1,-1)$.
- Right side: $pQ = 0.3\,(1,-1)Q = 0.3\,(-5)(1,-1) = -1.5\,(1,-1)$.
- Matching coefficients: $\dot c = -5c$, so $c(t) = 0.3\,e^{-5t}$.

So $p(t) = 0.3\,e^{-5t}\,(1,-1)$. At $t = 0.2$: $c = 0.3\,e^{-1} \approx 0.110$, so $p \approx (0.110, -0.110)$. The direction never moved; only the size shrank, with time constant $1/5$.

## What it hangs off

Two handles you already hold: the scalar solution $\dot c = \lambda c \Rightarrow c = c(0)e^{\lambda t}$, and the definition $vQ = \lambda v$ with $v \neq 0$. Nothing else was used. The next node (D2) asks: what if $p(0)$ is *not* along a single eigenvector? Answer: write it as a sum of eigenvectors and run this node on each piece.

title: Superposition: split p(0) into modes, let each decay on its own
body:
## Why we need this now

D1 solved the ODE $\dot p = pQ$ only in one special case: when $p(0)$ already points along a left eigenvector $v$. Then $p(t) = c(0)\,e^{\lambda t}\,v$. But a real starting distribution, say $p(0) = (1, 0)$ ("site starts closed"), almost never points along an eigenvector. So D1 alone is useless for actual initial conditions. We need a way to use it anyway.

## The move, and how you could have found it

Two facts you already own:

1. **The equation is linear.** If $p_1(t)$ and $p_2(t)$ both solve $\dot p = pQ$, then so does $p_1 + p_2$, because $(p_1+p_2)Q = p_1 Q + p_2 Q$. Matrix multiplication distributes over addition; that is the whole reason.
2. **D1:** along each eigenvector the solution is $c_i(0)\,e^{\lambda_i t}\,v_i$.

Put them together. If you can *write* $p(0)$ as a sum of eigenvectors,
$$p(0) = c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2 + \dots + c_n v_n,$$
then each piece evolves on its own by D1, and by linearity the sum of the evolved pieces is the solution:
$$p(t) = \sum_i c_i\, e^{\lambda_i t}\, v_i .$$

That is **superposition**. Nothing new was derived; we only noticed that linearity lets us add D1 solutions, and that finding the $c_i$ is just solving a linear system (expand $p(0)$ in the basis $\{v_i\}$).

The one thing this needs: the eigenvectors must **span** the space, so that *every* $p(0)$ can be written this way. For $n$ distinct eigenvalues this is automatic. Keep that condition in mind; it is the boundary of the method.

## Worked instance

$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$, eigenvalues $0$ and $-5$. You found the left eigenvectors before:
- $\lambda_1 = 0$: $v_1 = (4, 1)$ (check: $v_1 Q = (-4+4,\ 4-4) = (0,0)$).
- $\lambda_2 = -5$: $v_2 = (1, -1)$ (check: $v_2 Q = (-1-4,\ 1+4) = (-5, 5) = -5\,v_2$).

Start closed: $p(0) = (1, 0)$. Step 1, expand in the eigenbasis: solve $(1,0) = c_1 (4,1) + c_2 (1,-1)$.
Second component: $c_1 - c_2 = 0$, so $c_2 = c_1$. First component: $4c_1 + c_2 = 5c_1 = 1$, so $c_1 = c_2 = 0.2$.
Check: $0.2(4,1) + 0.2(1,-1) = (0.8+0.2,\ 0.2-0.2) = (1, 0)$. ✓

Step 2, let each mode go by D1:
$$p(t) = 0.2\,e^{0\cdot t}(4,1) + 0.2\,e^{-5t}(1,-1) = (0.8 + 0.2 e^{-5t},\ \ 0.2 - 0.2 e^{-5t}).$$

Read it: at $t=0$ it is $(1,0)$ ✓. As $t \to \infty$ the second mode dies and $p \to (0.8, 0.2)$, the stationary distribution (the $\lambda = 0$ eigenvector, normalised). The approach is a single exponential with rate $5 = |\lambda_2|$. Note the total $0.8+0.2 e^{-5t} + 0.2 - 0.2e^{-5t} = 1$ always: the decaying mode $(1,-1)$ sums to zero, so it moves probability around without creating or destroying it. That is exactly why you called it a deviation, not a population.

## What it hangs off

- **D1** gives each term $c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i$.
- **Linearity of $pQ$** lets you add the terms.
- **Spanning eigenvectors** lets you expand any $p(0)$ in the first place. Hold that one: the check next asks what happens when it fails.

title: When no coefficients exist: the expansion step can be inconsistent
body:
## The step that failed

You said: with only two eigenvectors in 3D, "finding the $c_i$ is no longer analytically solvable." The step is right, the reason is wrong, and the difference matters. The problem is not that the $c_i$ are hard to find. It is that for most $p(0)$ **no $c_i$ exist at all**. The linear system is inconsistent. Here is that, with numbers.

## Worked example

Suppose a 3-state $Q$ has only two independent left eigenvectors,
$$v_1 = (1, 0, 0), \qquad v_2 = (0, 1, 0).$$
We want to expand the initial distribution $p(0) = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$ as $c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2$.

**Move 1: write out the combination.** Any mixture of $v_1$ and $v_2$ is
$$c_1 (1,0,0) + c_2 (0,1,0) = (c_1,\ c_2,\ 0).$$
Reason: scalar times vector, then add component-wise. Note the third slot is $0$ no matter what $c_1, c_2$ are, because both eigenvectors have a $0$ there.

**Move 2: match components with $p(0)$.** Setting $(c_1, c_2, 0) = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$ gives three equations:
$$c_1 = 0.5, \qquad c_2 = 0.3, \qquad 0 = 0.2 .$$
Reason: two vectors are equal only if every component agrees.

**Move 3: read the third equation.** $0 = 0.2$ is false for every $c_1, c_2$. There is nothing to solve; the system has **no solution**. This is what "inconsistent" means: not hard, impossible.

**Move 4: say it geometrically.** $v_1$ and $v_2$ span the plane $z = 0$. Any $p(0)$ with a nonzero third component sits off that plane, and no mixture of in-plane vectors can leave the plane. So the superposition recipe cannot even start for such a $p(0)$. (The ODE still has a solution; it just is not a pure sum of exponentials, and contains a $t\,e^{\lambda t}$ term. We do not need that case for the LL chain.)

## Contrast: why the $2 \times 2$ case always worked

In the first reading, $v_1 = (4,1)$ and $v_2 = (1,-1)$ are two independent vectors in 2D. Two independent vectors in 2D span the whole plane, so for $p(0) = (1,0)$ the system
$$4c_1 + c_2 = 1, \qquad c_1 - c_2 = 0$$
had exactly one solution, $c_1 = c_2 = 0.2$. Same recipe, but here the count of independent eigenvectors equals the dimension. That count is the whole condition.

## The guarantee

When does an $n \times n$ matrix have $n$ independent eigenvectors? Always when its $n$ eigenvalues are **distinct**: eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are automatically independent. The 3-state LL chain has eigenvalues $0, \lambda_+, \lambda_-$ which are distinct for any positive rates, so superposition applies there without worry.

## What it hangs off

- Linearity of $pQ$ (lets us add modes) and D1 (evolves each mode).
- Plain vector algebra: equality of vectors is equality of every component. That is where the inconsistency shows up.

title: Why each coefficient obeys its own ċ = λc: the two-mode substitution
body:
## The step that failed

You can write $c_1(t) = c_1 e^{\lambda_1 t}$, but not say *why*. That is the memorized version. The understood version is one substitution, done once, and after that the formula is forced. Here it is with the numbers you already know.

## Setup

$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$, with $v_1 = (4,1)$, $\lambda_1 = 0$ and $v_2 = (1,-1)$, $\lambda_2 = -5$. Suppose at some time $p(t) = c_1(t)\, v_1 + c_2(t)\, v_2$ with the coefficients $c_1(t), c_2(t)$ **unknown functions**. The question is: what equations do they obey?

## Move 1: compute the right-hand side $pQ$

$$pQ = (c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2)\,Q = c_1\,(v_1 Q) + c_2\,(v_2 Q).$$
Reason: matrix multiplication distributes over addition and commutes with scalars. This is the *only* place linearity is used, and it is what lets the two terms be handled separately.

Now use the eigenvector property on each term: $v_1 Q = 0 \cdot v_1$ and $v_2 Q = -5\, v_2$. So
$$pQ = 0\cdot c_1\, v_1 + (-5)\, c_2\, v_2 .$$
Notice what happened: the $v_1$ term produced only a $v_1$ term, and the $v_2$ term only a $v_2$ term. Nothing crossed over. That is the eigenvector property at work.

## Move 2: compute the left-hand side $\dot p$

$v_1, v_2$ are constant vectors, so only the coefficients move:
$$\dot p = \dot c_1\, v_1 + \dot c_2\, v_2 .$$

## Move 3: equate, and match coefficients

The ODE says $\dot p = pQ$:
$$\dot c_1\, v_1 + \dot c_2\, v_2 = 0\cdot c_1\, v_1 + (-5)\, c_2\, v_2 .$$
Since $v_1 = (4,1)$ and $v_2 = (1,-1)$ are independent, a vector has only one way to be written as a combination of them, so the $v_1$ coefficients must agree and the $v_2$ coefficients must agree:
$$\dot c_1 = 0 \cdot c_1, \qquad \dot c_2 = -5\, c_2 .$$
Two separate scalar ODEs, one per mode, each of the form $\dot c = \lambda c$. This is D1, appearing once per eigenvector. The $v_2$ mode cannot feed into $\dot c_1$ because $v_2 Q$ has no $v_1$ component.

## Move 4: solve each

From the handle you own: $\dot c = \lambda c \Rightarrow c(t) = c(0) e^{\lambda t}$. So
$$c_1(t) = c_1(0)\, e^{0 \cdot t} = c_1(0), \qquad c_2(t) = c_2(0)\, e^{-5t}.$$
With $p(0) = (1,0)$ we found $c_1(0) = c_2(0) = 0.2$, giving $p(t) = 0.2\,(4,1) + 0.2\, e^{-5t}\,(1,-1)$, the same answer as before, now derived rather than quoted.

## The whole argument in one line

Substitute $p = \sum c_i v_i$ into $\dot p = pQ$; linearity plus $v_i Q = \lambda_i v_i$ turns the right side into $\sum \lambda_i c_i v_i$; independence of the $v_i$ lets you match coefficients to get $\dot c_i = \lambda_i c_i$ for each $i$. That is the sentence to be able to say.

title: e^{Qt}: the propagator, its series, and V^{-1} e^{Λt} V
body:
## Why this node now

D2 gives you a *recipe*: expand $p(0)$ in left eigenvectors, scale each coefficient by $e^{\lambda_i t}$, add back up. That works, but it is a procedure you rerun for every new $p(0)$. The question that leads to this node: **is there a single matrix that does the whole recipe at once**, so that $p(t) = p(0)\,M(t)$ for any start? There is, it is called $e^{Qt}$, and it is the answer to your side-chat question: $Q$ is the generator, $e^{Qt}$ is the propagator (the transition matrix over a finite time $t$), and $Qt$ by itself is neither.

## Discovery path 1: stack the slices

You already own $P(dt) = I + Q\,dt$ for one thin slice. Over a stretch $t$ cut into $n$ slices, the step matrices multiply:
$$P(t) = P(dt)^n = \Big(I + \frac{Qt}{n}\Big)^n .$$
This is exactly the compounding you did for the scalar case, $(1 - kt/n)^n \to e^{-kt}$, with the number $-k$ replaced by the matrix $Q$. The same limit, the same name:
$$e^{Qt} \;:=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\Big(I + \frac{Qt}{n}\Big)^n \;=\; I + Qt + \frac{Q^2 t^2}{2!} + \frac{Q^3 t^3}{3!} + \cdots$$
The series is the definition. Two checks that it is the right object:
- At $t = 0$ it is $I$: nothing has happened yet.
- Differentiate the series term by term: $\frac{d}{dt}e^{Qt} = Q + Q^2 t + \frac{Q^3 t^2}{2!} + \cdots = Q\,e^{Qt}$. So $p(t) = p(0)e^{Qt}$ obeys $\dot p = p(0)\,Q e^{Qt}$. Since every term in the series is a power of $Q$, $Q$ commutes with $e^{Qt}$, so this is $p(0)e^{Qt}Q = p(t)Q$. It solves the master equation for every $p(0)$.

One warning that will come back: $e^{Qt}$ is **not** the matrix of entrywise exponentials $e^{Q_{ij}t}$. The series mixes entries through the powers $Q^2, Q^3, \dots$.

## Discovery path 2: the series is the mode recipe in disguise

Why should the series agree with D2? Stack the left-eigenvector equations $v_i Q = \lambda_i v_i$ as rows: let $V$ be the matrix whose rows are $v_1, v_2$, and $\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2)$. Then
$$VQ = \Lambda V \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = V^{-1}\Lambda V ,$$
where $V^{-1}$ exists exactly because the $v_i$ are independent (the same condition that let you match coefficients in D2). Now powers collapse: $Q^2 = V^{-1}\Lambda V V^{-1}\Lambda V = V^{-1}\Lambda^2 V$, and in general $Q^k = V^{-1}\Lambda^k V$. Put that into the series, pull $V^{-1}$ and $V$ outside the sum:
$$e^{Qt} = V^{-1}\Big(\sum_k \frac{\Lambda^k t^k}{k!}\Big)V = V^{-1} e^{\Lambda t}\,V, \qquad e^{\Lambda t} = \mathrm{diag}(e^{\lambda_1 t}, e^{\lambda_2 t}).$$
Read it right to left as a story: $V^{-1}$ turns $p(0)$ into mode coefficients, $e^{\Lambda t}$ scales each coefficient by its own $e^{\lambda_i t}$, $V$ adds the modes back up. Exactly D2, written as one matrix.

## Worked instance

$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $v_1 = (1,2)$ with $\lambda_1 = 0$, $v_2 = (1,-1)$ with $\lambda_2 = -3$.

**Step 1, build $V$ and $V^{-1}$.** $V = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\det V = -1 - 2 = -3$, so
$$V^{-1} = \frac{1}{-3}\begin{pmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/3 & 2/3 \\ 1/3 & -1/3 \end{pmatrix}.$$
Check: row 1 of $V$ times $V^{-1}$ is $(1/3 + 2/3,\; 2/3 - 2/3) = (1, 0)$. Good.

**Step 2, $e^{\Lambda t} = \mathrm{diag}(1, e^{-3t})$.** Write $\epsilon = e^{-3t}$ to keep the algebra readable.

**Step 3, multiply.** $V^{-1} e^{\Lambda t} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/3 & \tfrac{2}{3}\epsilon \\ 1/3 & -\tfrac{1}{3}\epsilon \end{pmatrix}$, then times $V$:
$$e^{Qt} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 1 + 2\epsilon & 2 - 2\epsilon \\ 1 - \epsilon & 2 + \epsilon \end{pmatrix}.$$

**Step 4, three sanity checks** (do these every time; they catch most errors):
- $t = 0$, so $\epsilon = 1$: $\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = I$. Good.
- Each row sums to $1$: $(1 + 2\epsilon + 2 - 2\epsilon)/3 = 1$. Probability conserved, as rows of $Q$ summing to zero demand.
- $t \to \infty$, so $\epsilon \to 0$: both rows become $(1/3, 2/3)$, the stationary split $v_1/3$. Every start forgets where it began.

**Step 5, use it.** Start in state 1, $p(0) = (1, 0)$: $p(t)$ is row 1,
$$p(t) = \Big(\tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{2}{3}e^{-3t},\; \tfrac{2}{3} - \tfrac{2}{3}e^{-3t}\Big).$$
Compare with the D2 recipe: $(1,0) = c_1(1,2) + c_2(1,-1)$ gives $c_1 = 1/3$, $c_2 = 2/3$, so $p(t) = \tfrac{1}{3}(1,2) + \tfrac{2}{3}e^{-3t}(1,-1)$, the same vector. The matrix did the recipe for you, and row $i$ of $e^{Qt}$ is simply $p(t)$ for the pure start in state $i$.

## What it hangs off

- The series hangs off $P(dt) = I + Q\,dt$ and the compounding limit you did for $e^{-kt}$.
- The factorisation $V^{-1} e^{\Lambda t} V$ hangs off D1 ($v_i Q = \lambda_i v_i$, stacked into $VQ = \Lambda V$) and on the independence of the $v_i$, which is what makes $V^{-1}$ exist. If $Q$ is defective (D2's boundary case), $V$ is not square-invertible and this formula is unavailable, but the series still is.

title: The matrix exponential: one object that carries all the modes at once
body:
## What this section is about

Superposition solves $\dot p = pQ$ mode by mode: expand $p(0) = \sum_i c_i v_i$ in left eigenvectors ($v_i Q = \lambda_i v_i$), then $p(t) = \sum_i c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i$. That is a *recipe*. This section packages the recipe into a single matrix, $e^{Qt}$, so that the whole solution is one multiplication:

$$p(t) = p(0)\, e^{Qt}.$$

The payoff: $e^{Qt}$ is exactly the propagator $P(t)$ you already know from the chain, its entries are the transition probabilities over a time $t$, and later it lets us read $k_{obs}$ straight off the eigenvalues.

## Why we need it

The recipe has a hidden step. Substituting $p = c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2$ into $\dot p = pQ$ gives one vector equation, $\dot c_1 v_1 + \dot c_2 v_2 = \lambda_1 c_1 v_1 + \lambda_2 c_2 v_2$, and we split it into two scalar ones, $\dot c_i = \lambda_i c_i$. What allows the split is that $v_1, v_2$ are **linearly independent**: a vector has only one expansion in an independent set, so equal vectors have equal coefficients. (Linearity of $pQ$ did a different job earlier: it let $pQ$ be spread over the sum as $c_1 v_1 Q + c_2 v_2 Q$. It does not justify matching.) Once the modes are independent, the recipe is a *linear map* from $p(0)$ to $p(t)$, and every linear map on row vectors is multiplication by some matrix. Let us find that matrix.

## How you could have discovered it

For the scalar equation $\dot c = \lambda c$ the solution is $c(0)e^{\lambda t}$, and the exponential is the power series

$$e^{\lambda t} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda t)^k}{k!}.$$

The only thing that series uses about $\lambda$ is that you can multiply it by itself. A square matrix can also be multiplied by itself. So *define*

$$e^{Qt} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(Qt)^k}{k!} = I + Qt + \frac{Q^2 t^2}{2} + \cdots$$

Does it solve the matrix equation? Differentiate term by term: $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{Q^k t^k}{k!} = \frac{Q^k t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}$, so the derivative of the series is $Q(I + Qt + \cdots) = Q\,e^{Qt}$, and also $e^{Qt}Q$ (every term is a power of $Q$, so $Q$ commutes with all of them). Hence $p(t) = p(0)e^{Qt}$ satisfies $\dot p = p(0)e^{Qt}Q = pQ$ with $p(0)$ at $t=0$, because the series at $t=0$ is $I$. This is the solution.

Now connect it to the modes. Hit the series with a left eigenvector: $v_i Q^k = \lambda_i^k v_i$ (apply $v_i Q = \lambda_i v_i$ $k$ times), so

$$v_i\, e^{Qt} = \sum_k \frac{t^k}{k!}\lambda_i^k v_i = e^{\lambda_i t} v_i.$$

Each mode just gets multiplied by its own scalar exponential. Then for a general $p(0) = \sum_i c_i v_i$,

$$p(0)e^{Qt} = \sum_i c_i\, v_i e^{Qt} = \sum_i c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i,$$

which is the superposition formula word for word. **So $e^{Qt}$ is the superposition recipe written as a matrix.** Nothing new was added; the series is just a way of writing the same map without naming the modes.

## The closed form $V^{-1} e^{\Lambda t} V$

Stack the left eigenvectors as the rows of a matrix $V$, and put the eigenvalues on a diagonal $\Lambda$. The $n$ eigenvector equations $v_i Q = \lambda_i v_i$ become one matrix equation, $VQ = \Lambda V$. If the $v_i$ are independent, $V$ is invertible, and

$$Q = V^{-1}\Lambda V, \qquad Q^k = V^{-1}\Lambda^k V$$

(the inner $V V^{-1}$ pairs cancel). Feed that into the series:

$$e^{Qt} = V^{-1}\Big(\sum_k \frac{\Lambda^k t^k}{k!}\Big)V = V^{-1} e^{\Lambda t} V, \qquad e^{\Lambda t} = \mathrm{diag}(e^{\lambda_1 t},\dots,e^{\lambda_n t}).$$

Reading it right to left: $V$ decomposes $p(0)$ into mode coefficients ($p(0) = cV$ means $c = p(0)V^{-1}$), $e^{\Lambda t}$ lets each mode decay at its own rate, $V^{-1}$ reassembles the vector. Same three steps as the recipe.

## Worked instance

$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -3 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, left eigenvectors $v_1 = (1,3)$ with $\lambda_1 = 0$ and $v_2 = (1,-1)$ with $\lambda_2 = -4$. (Check one: $(1,-1)Q = (-3-1,\ 3+1) = (-4, 4) = -4\,(1,-1)$.)

**Step 1, build $V$ and $\Lambda$.** Rows are the eigenvectors: $V = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(0,-4)$.

**Step 2, invert $V$.** $\det V = (1)(-1) - (3)(1) = -4$, so $V^{-1} = \frac{1}{-4}\begin{pmatrix} -1 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/4 & 3/4 \\ 1/4 & -1/4 \end{pmatrix}$. (Check: first row of $V$ times first column of $V^{-1}$ is $1/4 + 3/4 = 1$.)

**Step 3, multiply.** $V^{-1}e^{\Lambda t} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/4 & \tfrac34 e^{-4t} \\ 1/4 & -\tfrac14 e^{-4t} \end{pmatrix}$ (each column of $V^{-1}$ scaled by its exponential). Then times $V$:

$$e^{Qt} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac14 + \tfrac34 e^{-4t} & \tfrac34 - \tfrac34 e^{-4t} \\ \tfrac14 - \tfrac14 e^{-4t} & \tfrac34 + \tfrac14 e^{-4t} \end{pmatrix}.$$

**Step 4, sanity checks, each one a reason to trust it.** At $t = 0$ it is the identity (nothing has happened yet). Each row sums to 1 (probability is conserved; this is the $\lambda_1 = 0$ mode). As $t\to\infty$ every row tends to $(1/4, 3/4)$, which is $v_1$ normalised: whatever you start in, you forget it and land on the stationary split. And the derivative at $t=0$ of the top row is $(-3, 3)$, the first row of $Q$: for small $t$, $e^{Qt} \approx I + Qt$, the one-slice transition matrix. So the entry $(e^{Qt})_{ij}$ is the probability of being in state $j$ at time $t$ having started in state $i$. **$e^{Qt}$ is the propagator $P(t)$, and $Q$ is its generator.**

## What it hangs off

Two things you already own. The scalar fact $\dot c = \lambda c \Rightarrow c(0)e^{\lambda t}$, whose series we copied with $Q$ in place of $\lambda$. And superposition, $p(t) = \sum_i c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i$, which is what $p(0)e^{Qt}$ expands to once you apply $v_i Q^k = \lambda_i^k v_i$ term by term. The one new ingredient is that independence of the $v_i$ makes $V$ invertible, which is exactly what $V^{-1}$ needs.

title: The spectrum of the 3-state Linderstrøm-Lang chain
body:
## What this section is about

The Linderstrøm-Lang chain is the three-state model behind hydrogen-deuterium exchange: a site is **closed** ($C$, protected), opens to **open** ($O$, exposed) at rate $k_{op}$, closes back at $k_{cl}$, and from the open state exchanges irreversibly at the chemical rate $k_{ch}$ into **exchanged** ($E$). This section finds the eigenvalues of its rate matrix. Those three numbers are the whole story of the kinetics: by the matrix exponential, every population is a sum of $e^{\lambda_i t}$ terms, so the eigenvalues are the only rates that can ever appear in a measured uptake curve.

## Why we need it now

We have $p(t) = p(0)e^{Qt} = \sum_i c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i$. For the chain, $p = (p_C, p_O, p_E)$ and what you measure is the unexchanged fraction $U(t) = p_C + p_O = 1 - p_E$. So $U(t)$ is a sum of exponentials with the eigenvalues of $Q$ as the decay rates. The question "what is $k_{obs}$?" is literally "what is the slowest nonzero eigenvalue?" We cannot answer it until we have the spectrum.

## Build the generator

Rows are "from", columns are "to", off-diagonal entries are jump rates, diagonals are minus the total exit rate so every row sums to zero (conservation). With the ordering $(C, O, E)$:

$$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -k_{op} & k_{op} & 0 \\ k_{cl} & -(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) & k_{ch} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$

The last row is all zeros because $E$ is absorbing: nothing leaves it.

## How you could have found the eigenvalues

Eigenvalues are the roots of $\det(Q - \lambda I) = 0$. Before expanding anything, look at the shape. The third row of $Q - \lambda I$ is $(0, 0, -\lambda)$. Expanding the determinant along that row gives

$$\det(Q - \lambda I) = -\lambda \cdot \det(A - \lambda I), \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix} -k_{op} & k_{op} \\ k_{cl} & -(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) \end{pmatrix}.$$

So one eigenvalue is $\lambda_0 = 0$ **immediately**, and it is the absorbing state's: the left eigenvector is $v_0 = (0,0,1)$ (check: $(0,0,1)Q$ is the zero row). This is the stationary split, everything exchanged. The other two eigenvalues come from the $2\times 2$ block $A$, which is just the $C \rightleftharpoons O$ system with an extra leak $k_{ch}$ out of $O$.

For a $2\times 2$ matrix, $\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$. Here

$$\operatorname{tr} A = -(k_{op} + k_{cl} + k_{ch}) \equiv -S, \qquad \det A = k_{op}(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) - k_{op}k_{cl} = k_{op}k_{ch} \equiv P.$$

Notice the cancellation in the determinant: the $k_{op}k_{cl}$ terms kill each other and only the *product of the two rates along the exit path* survives, $k_{op}k_{ch}$. The characteristic equation is

$$\lambda^2 + S\lambda + P = 0, \qquad \lambda_\pm = \frac{-S \pm \sqrt{S^2 - 4P}}{2}.$$

Both roots are real and negative: $S^2 - 4P = (k_{op} - k_{ch})^2 + k_{cl}^2 + 2k_{cl}(k_{op}+k_{ch}) > 0$, and since $S > 0$ and $P > 0$ both roots have negative real part (sum $-S$, product $P$). So the spectrum is $\{0, \lambda_-, \lambda_+\}$ with $\lambda_- < \lambda_+ < 0$. One mode is stationary, one is fast, one is slow.

## The approximation you will actually use

In HDX, $P = k_{op}k_{ch}$ is almost always tiny compared to $S^2$ (opening is rare, or closing is fast, or both). For a quadratic with $P \ll S^2$, the two roots are very unequal and you can read them off without the square root. The product of the roots is $P$ and their sum is $-S$: if one root is tiny, the other must carry the whole sum, so

$$\lambda_{\text{fast}} \approx -S, \qquad \lambda_{\text{slow}} \approx -\frac{P}{S} = -\frac{k_{op}k_{ch}}{k_{op}+k_{cl}+k_{ch}}.$$

(Same thing from the square root: $\sqrt{S^2 - 4P} \approx S - 2P/S$ to first order.) The slow one is the rate the experiment sees over long times, and when $k_{op} \ll k_{cl} + k_{ch}$ it reduces to the formula you already carry: $k_{obs} = \dfrac{k_{op}k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$.

## Worked instance

Take $k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10$ (all per second).

**Step 1, $S$ and $P$.** $S = 1 + 100 + 10 = 111$. $P = 1 \times 10 = 10$. (Only the product along the exit path enters $P$; $k_{cl}$ shows up in $S$ alone.)

**Step 2, discriminant.** $S^2 - 4P = 12321 - 40 = 12281$, $\sqrt{12281} \approx 110.82$. The $4P$ is a tiny correction under the root: the roots are going to be very unequal.

**Step 3, roots.** $\lambda_+ = \frac{-111 + 110.82}{2} \approx -0.090$ per second, $\lambda_- = \frac{-111 - 110.82}{2} \approx -110.9$ per second.

**Step 4, check against the shortcut.** $-P/S = -10/111 = -0.0901$. Agrees to three figures. And the familiar $k_{op}k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) = 10/110 = 0.0909$, off by one percent because it drops $k_{op}$ from the denominator. Fast mode: $-S = -111$ versus the exact $-110.9$.

**Step 5, read it.** The spectrum is $\{0, -0.09, -111\}$. Within about $1/111 \approx 0.01$ s the fast mode is gone: the $C \rightleftharpoons O$ pre-equilibrium has settled. After that, the unexchanged fraction decays as a single exponential with $k_{obs} \approx 0.09$ per second, a thousandfold slower. title: The spectrum of the 3-state Linderstrøm-Lang chain
body:
## What this section is about

The Linderstrøm-Lang chain is the three-state model behind hydrogen-deuterium exchange: a site is **closed** ($C$, protected), opens to **open** ($O$, exposed) at rate $k_{op}$, closes back at $k_{cl}$, and from the open state exchanges irreversibly at the chemical rate $k_{ch}$ into **exchanged** ($E$). This section finds the eigenvalues of its rate matrix. Those three numbers are the whole story of the kinetics: by the matrix exponential, every population is a sum of $e^{\lambda_i t}$ terms, so the eigenvalues are the only rates that can ever appear in a measured uptake curve.

## Why we need it now

We have $p(t) = p(0)e^{Qt} = \sum_i c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i$. For the chain, $p = (p_C, p_O, p_E)$ and what you measure is the unexchanged fraction $U(t) = p_C + p_O = 1 - p_E$. So $U(t)$ is a sum of exponentials with the eigenvalues of $Q$ as the decay rates. The question "what is $k_{obs}$?" is literally "what is the slowest nonzero eigenvalue?" We cannot answer it until we have the spectrum.

## Build the generator

Rows are "from", columns are "to", off-diagonal entries are jump rates, diagonals are minus the total exit rate so every row sums to zero (conservation). With the ordering $(C, O, E)$:

$$Q = \begin{pmatrix} -k_{op} & k_{op} & 0 \\ k_{cl} & -(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) & k_{ch} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$

The last row is all zeros because $E$ is absorbing: nothing leaves it.

## How you could have found the eigenvalues

Eigenvalues are the roots of $\det(Q - \lambda I) = 0$. Before expanding anything, look at the shape. The third row of $Q - \lambda I$ is $(0, 0, -\lambda)$. Expanding the determinant along that row gives

$$\det(Q - \lambda I) = -\lambda \cdot \det(A - \lambda I), \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix} -k_{op} & k_{op} \\ k_{cl} & -(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) \end{pmatrix}.$$

So one eigenvalue is $\lambda_0 = 0$ **immediately**, and it is the absorbing state's: the left eigenvector is $v_0 = (0,0,1)$ (check: $(0,0,1)Q$ is the zero row). This is the stationary split, everything exchanged. The other two eigenvalues come from the $2\times 2$ block $A$, which is just the $C \rightleftharpoons O$ system with an extra leak $k_{ch}$ out of $O$.

For a $2\times 2$ matrix, $\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$. Here

$$\operatorname{tr} A = -(k_{op} + k_{cl} + k_{ch}) \equiv -S, \qquad \det A = k_{op}(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) - k_{op}k_{cl} = k_{op}k_{ch} \equiv P.$$

Notice the cancellation in the determinant: the $k_{op}k_{cl}$ terms kill each other and only the *product of the two rates along the exit path* survives, $k_{op}k_{ch}$. The characteristic equation is

$$\lambda^2 + S\lambda + P = 0, \qquad \lambda_\pm = \frac{-S \pm \sqrt{S^2 - 4P}}{2}.$$

Both roots are real and negative: $S^2 - 4P = (k_{op} - k_{ch})^2 + k_{cl}^2 + 2k_{cl}(k_{op}+k_{ch}) > 0$, and since $S > 0$ and $P > 0$ both roots are negative (sum $-S$, product $P$). So the spectrum is $\{0, \lambda_-, \lambda_+\}$ with $\lambda_- < \lambda_+ < 0$. One mode is stationary, one is fast, one is slow.

## The approximation you will actually use

In HDX, $P = k_{op}k_{ch}$ is almost always tiny compared to $S^2$ (opening is rare, or closing is fast, or both). For a quadratic with $P \ll S^2$, the two roots are very unequal and you can read them off without the square root. The product of the roots is $P$ and their sum is $-S$: if one root is tiny, the other must carry the whole sum, so

$$\lambda_{\text{fast}} \approx -S, \qquad \lambda_{\text{slow}} \approx -\frac{P}{S} = -\frac{k_{op}k_{ch}}{k_{op}+k_{cl}+k_{ch}}.$$

(Same thing from the square root: $\sqrt{S^2 - 4P} \approx S - 2P/S$ to first order.) The slow one is the rate the experiment sees over long times, and when $k_{op} \ll k_{cl} + k_{ch}$ it reduces to the formula you already carry: $k_{obs} = \dfrac{k_{op}k_{ch}}{k_{cl}+k_{ch}}$.

## Worked instance

Take $k_{op} = 1$, $k_{cl} = 100$, $k_{ch} = 10$ (all per second).

**Step 1, $S$ and $P$.** $S = 1 + 100 + 10 = 111$. $P = 1 \times 10 = 10$. (Only the product along the exit path enters $P$; $k_{cl}$ shows up in $S$ alone.)

**Step 2, discriminant.** $S^2 - 4P = 12321 - 40 = 12281$, $\sqrt{12281} \approx 110.82$. The $4P$ is a tiny correction under the root: the roots are going to be very unequal.

**Step 3, roots.** $\lambda_+ = \frac{-111 + 110.82}{2} \approx -0.090$ per second, $\lambda_- = \frac{-111 - 110.82}{2} \approx -110.9$ per second.

**Step 4, check against the shortcut.** $-P/S = -10/111 = -0.0901$. Agrees to three figures. And the familiar $k_{op}k_{ch}/(k_{cl}+k_{ch}) = 10/110 = 0.0909$, off by one percent because it drops $k_{op}$ from the denominator. Fast mode: $-S = -111$ versus the exact $-110.9$.

**Step 5, read it.** The spectrum is $\{0, -0.09, -111\}$. Within about $1/111 \approx 0.01$ s the fast mode is gone: the $C \rightleftharpoons O$ pre-equilibrium has settled. After that, the unexchanged fraction decays as a single exponential with $k_{obs} \approx 0.09$ per second, a thousandfold slower. The ratio $\lambda_-/\lambda_+ \approx 1200$ is what makes the one-exponential description of HDX work.
